newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malayan Banking year net seen up 27 pct.
newsitem.headline: Malayan Banking year net seen up 27 pct.

text.p: Maybank, Malaysia's largest commercial bank, is expected to post another year of strong earnings gains, boosted by continuing rapid loans growth, said banking analysts on Tuesday.

A poll of 34 research houses by Edinburgh Financial Publications Estimate Directory showed an average estimated net profit of 1.37 billion ringgit ($489.3 million) for the year to June 30, 1997, against 1.08 billion ringgit for the same period in 1996, an expected rise of around 27 percent.
Analysts expect the bank to release its results on August 26.
Powering the bank's growth is an expected increase in total loans of between 15 and 20 percent for the year, said analysts. Maybank's total loans grew by 16.4 percent in the preceding period.
"The bank's profits are mainly driven by loans growth of around 15 to 20 percent," said Soon Teck Onn, banking analyst at ING Barings in Kuala Lumpur.
Maybank's existing loans and advances amount to 56.46 billion ringgit, according to its 1996 annual report.

Even though this is slightly below the Malaysian banking industry's average loans growth rate, most of the other 36 commercial banks in Malaysia are growing from much smaller loans and deposits bases, said analysts.

The recent storm in Southeast Asian currencies which has resulted in the ringgit hitting new lows against the U.S. dollar since it was floated in 1973, and the resulting increase in interbank lending rates, has so far not affected Maybank significantly, said analysts.
In July, Maybank increased its base lending rate to 9.35 percent from 9.10 percent.
"I don't think there will be much impact from the ringgit's weakness, as it does not have any major U.S. dollar exposure," said Soon.
Maybank has several advantages over its competitors, the main one being its sheer size, analysts said.
"Maybank has a market share of around 70 to 80 percent of the total customer deposits of the industry," said a banking analyst at a foreign equities research house in Kuala Lumpur.
It has the country's largest branch network, exceeding 200, he said.
The sale of its 75 percent stake in Kwong Yik Bank Bhd in November 1996 yielded Maybank 2.16 billion ringgit, and gave it a large pool of practically cost-free money to lend, said analysts.
Maybank's diversity of its loan portfolio is another attractive feature, said analysts.

Its exposure to property and share financing, two areas Malaysian authorities have been trying to control for the best part of the last year, is far below guidelines stipulated by the central Bank Negara, said analysts.
Housing loans comprise 15 percent of its total loans, while share financing takes up eight percent, said the foreign banking analyst.
Manufacturing and trade finance form the bulk of its loans, accounting for around 35 percent, giving the bank a large exposure to Malaysia's most productive sectors.

Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, said in March that commercial banks could only lend up to 20 percent of their overall outstanding loans for property purchases and 15 percent for financing share purchases.
($1=2.8 ringgit)
